headline: Before AlphaFold, Demis Hassabis Built Games About Seizing Power
lede: The CEO of Google DeepMind and co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry spent his late twenties running a studio whose two finished games were a simulation of covertly taking over a fictional post-Soviet state and a tongue-in-cheek supervillain lair-manager. An observation circulating in an AI-safety-adjacent thread finds it remarkable that this biographical detail goes largely unremarked. The irony is real; the specific game list cited is not quite right.
body:
**Demis Hassabis** is today the CEO of Google DeepMind (GOOGL) — the entity formed in 2023 when Alphabet merged its two preeminent AI research labs — and co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for *AlphaFold*, a system that predicted the three-dimensional shape of virtually every known protein. Before any of that, he founded Elixir Studios, a London-based games developer, in 1998, and over seven years shipped exactly two titles.

The first, *Republic: The Revolution* (2003), placed the player inside Novistrana, a detailed fictional post-Soviet state, tasked with accumulating factions, bribing officials, and staging demonstrations until enough political leverage existed to unseat the incumbent regime — surreptitiously, by design. The second, *Evil Genius* (2004), was a *real-time strategy* base-builder in which the player managed a secret island lair, recruited henchmen, and fended off a Bond-style international task force — the tone deliberately camp, the mechanics genuinely polished. *Evil Genius* acquired a devoted cult following; *Republic* sold poorly and was judged ambitious but broken. Elixir folded in April 2005, after a third, unannounced project was cancelled mid-development.

The screenshot attributes three games to Hassabis, adding *Black & White* — the 2001 god-simulator from Lionhead Studios — to the pair above. This is wrong, though the confusion is understandable. Hassabis joined Lionhead in 1997 as lead AI programmer and was present during the early conceptual phase of *Black & White*. He departed in 1998 to found Elixir, three years before the game shipped. *Black & White* was Peter Molyneux's project from start to finish; the creature AI that became its signature feature was built by specialist Richard Evans after Hassabis had already left. Calling him its maker conflates an early staffing credit with authorship of the work.

The fuller arc is, if anything, more striking than the screenshot's version. Hassabis was hired at sixteen by Molyneux to co-design *Theme Park* (1994) at Bullfrog Productions — a foundational title in the *management simulation* genre — before stepping away to complete a computer science degree at Cambridge. He has said in multiple interviews that game development was always instrumental, a route into AI rather than a destination in itself. After Elixir's closure he enrolled in a PhD in cognitive neuroscience at University College London, studying how the hippocampus reconstructs stored memories into imagined future scenarios, a line of inquiry that directly informed his interest in how AI systems model and plan. He co-founded DeepMind in 2010 with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman; Google (GOOGL) acquired it in 2014.

The games were commercial entertainment products in well-worn genres, not manifestos. *Evil Genius* is an explicit Bond-villain parody; *Republic* was an earnest political simulation that happened to find too few buyers. If the arc invites a raised eyebrow, it is perhaps less that the studio's two games were *about* power than that Hassabis has been unusually consistent, over two decades, in describing *artificial general intelligence* as the project he was always building toward — and in publicly acknowledging that its risks are serious. The irony of his back-catalogue is worth a sentence. Treating it as a missed structural clue to something darker requires a rather liberal interpretation of genre.

concepts.definition: A video game genre in which players build bases, gather resources, and command units in continuous time rather than in discrete turns. Evil Genius uses the genre's base-building mechanics but frames them around managing a supervillain's secret lair.

A game genre in which the player constructs and runs a complex system — a theme park, a hospital, a city — balancing competing demands over time. Theme Park (1994), co-designed by Hassabis at Bullfrog, is widely credited with founding the modern form of the genre.

A deep-learning system developed by Google DeepMind that predicts the three-dimensional structure of a protein from its amino acid sequence. Released in 2020–21, it solved a fifty-year-old grand challenge in structural biology and earned Hassabis and colleague John Jumper the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

A hypothetical AI system capable of performing any intellectual task a human can, rather than excelling in one narrow domain. It is the long-standing research goal Hassabis has cited publicly as DeepMind's founding ambition, and it remains contested among researchers as a concept and a target.

A cognitive neuroscience framework, developed in part through Hassabis's PhD research at UCL, proposing that the hippocampus does not merely store memories but recombines them to construct simulations of possible futures. The theory connects biological memory to the capacity for imagination and planning — themes Hassabis later carried into AI architecture research.

fact_check: The screenshot credits Hassabis with three games: Black & White, Republic: The Revolution, and Evil Genius. Black & White should not be on that list. Hassabis was lead AI programmer at Lionhead Studios during the game's early pre-production in 1997–98, then left to found Elixir. Black & White shipped in March 2001 under Peter Molyneux's direction; its creature AI was developed by Richard Evans. The correct count of games Hassabis made as a studio founder is two: Republic: The Revolution and Evil Genius. He also co-designed Theme Park at sixteen at Bullfrog Productions, but that predates Elixir entirely. Calling him the maker of Black & White conflates a brief early staffing credit with authorship of the finished work.
